name: Avail
label: Lookout!
lede: A Reston hardcore band moved into a Richmond rowhouse in 1990, handed the drummer the microphone, recruited a bassist from a laundromat, and spent the next decade writing Richmond into song titles while a shirtless cheerleader broke bones in the pit.

eras.title: Reston kids, Richmond rowhouse
eras.text: Avail began as a suburban hardcore band in Reston, Virginia, in the long shadow of D.C. Around 1990 Joe Banks gave up on the D.C. area, moved the band into a Richmond rowhouse, and drummer Tim Barry moved to the microphone.

years.h: Avail forms in Reston, Virginia
years.p: Guitarist [[Joe Banks|e7e35c4c-475b-4c7e-9671-893312c16ad5]], singer Brien Stewart, drummer Doug Crosby and bassist Mikey Warstler start Avail in the Northern Virginia suburbs. Banks is the only founder still in the band.

years.src: Wikipedia: Who's to Say What Stays the Same · Fat Wreck Chords
years.h: Avail cuts its first vinyl at Inner Ear, with Tim Barry on drums
years.p: Brien Stewart sings, Joe Banks plays guitar, D.J. Grimes plays bass and [[Tim Barry|300184e2-cb52-478c-9541-a6d0db1b7257]], formerly of rival band Learning Disabled Kids, plays drums at Inner Ear Studio.
years.xp:
The four songs first came out on the 1990 cassette Reaching Out, then as the Who's to Say What Stays the Same EP on SunSpot Records in May 1991, Avail's first vinyl. Banks produced it.

Wikipedia credits Barry with drums on the session. Fat Wreck Chords' band bio says he joined as the drummer and moved to the microphone around 1990.

years.h: Avail gives up on D.C. and moves into a Richmond rowhouse
years.p: Joe Banks relocated Avail to Richmond, Virginia, in 1990, and Tim Barry moved from the drum stool to the microphone. From then on, Richmond was what Avail's songs were about.
years.xp: Fat Wreck Chords' bio says the band gave up on the D.C. area in 1990 and took a historic Richmond rowhouse to get serious. By 2003, Barry told Razorcake, Avail had practiced in Banks's house for nine years, and Banks had since bought it.

eras.title: Phone lists and Lookout!
eras.text: Avail spent these years learning to tour, one borrowed phone number at a time, and landing on Lookout! Records, the Berkeley label that had put out Green Day's first records. Two Lookout! albums made in a Silver Spring, Maryland studio put Richmond on the map for punks everywhere else.

years.src: Wikipedia: Satiate · Discogs · Razorcake #14 · Wikipedia: Live at the Kings Head Inn
years.h: Satiate, Avail's debut, on Catheter-Assembly
years.p: Avail's first album came out on Adam Thompson's Catheter-Assembly label, then on Old Glory, then on Lookout! CD in 1994. The song Mr. Morgan is about an elderly Richmond man killed in a robbery.
years.xp:
Tracked in September and October 1991 at Gizmo and Wolftrack studios with Chuck McCauley on bass and [[Erik Larson|d29befcc-6291-46c9-873e-bf477f0de6b6]] on drums. The credits list Beau Beau as Cheerleader, his job title ever since.

Lookout!'s 1994 CD added two songs from the 1993 Attempt to Regress 7-inch. That same year Old Glory put out Live at the Kings Head Inn, taped in Norfolk, Virginia, in April 1993.

years.h: Born Against's Adam Nathanson hands Tim Barry a phone list
years.p: [[Born Against|983825cd-4c25-45c5-adbb-3f9cdced6285]]'s Adam Nathanson sent Tim Barry the phone numbers from Born Against's own tours, and Avail built its first real tour from them.
years.xp: Before that, Barry told Razorcake, Avail played two out-of-state shows and called it a tour. Years later the band was booking tours of 160 dates.

years.h: Dixie on Lookout!, with a John Mellencamp cover
years.p: Avail recorded Dixie in June 1994 with Larry Packer at Uncle Punchy Studios in Silver Spring, Maryland. Twelve originals plus Mellencamp's Pink Houses.
years.xp: The line-up was Tim Barry, Joe Banks, Chuck McCauley, Erik Larson and Beau Beau. Barry has named Springsteen and Mellencamp as models for writing about everyday life until it turns political.

years.h: Tim Barry doubles as bassist in (Young) Pioneers
years.p: From 1994 to 1995 Tim Barry also played bass in the Richmond folk-punk band [[(Young) Pioneers|642ef2de-0d93-45aa-a27c-a93f32ebfbbb]], who shared the 1997 Lookout! split The Fall of Richmond with Avail.

years.h: 4am Friday is named for the hour Bob Baynor's death reached Avail
years.p: Avail titled its third album for the day and time it got news that Bob Baynor of [[Maximillian Colby|ed0c2410-784d-489e-864e-17c3ebeffd7d]] had died in 1995. The song F.C.A. is Avail's tribute to him.
years.xp:
Baynor played bass in Maximillian Colby, a band formed at James Madison University in Harrisonburg, Virginia; Lovitt Records says his death in 1995 brought that band to a halt. No source found gives a cause.

Recorded January to February 1996 at Uncle Punchy with Rob Kelshian on bass. One track was sung by Ben Winkler, the sleeve says, at a rest stop off the New Jersey Turnpike. Simple Song later landed on Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 4.

eras.title: Over the James and a third of the year in a van
eras.text: A homeless kid from a laundromat became the bassist, and Avail made Over the James, the record Decibel would later call a melodic hardcore classic. Then came Fat Wreck Chords, a muralist on drums, and tours so long the band lived a third of every year in the van.

years.src: Decibel Hall of Fame extras · No Echo
years.h: Tim Barry finds Gwomper homeless in a Richmond laundromat
years.p: After a bassist quit on a European tour, Tim Barry found Justin "Gwomper" Burdick sitting in a Richmond laundromat with his clothes in a trash bag. Gwomper had never played bass.
years.xp:
Avail handed him a classical guitar to learn the songs on while it toured Europe for five weeks, and he switched to bass when the band came home. Gwomper told Decibel he had been saving for a winter in Colorado, lost the money, and came back to Richmond instead.

He credits Chuck McCauley, who played bass on Satiate and Dixie, for teaching him the parts.

years.src: Wikipedia: Over the James · Decibel · Pitchfork
years.h: Over the James: Richmond's streets become song titles
years.p: Recorded in December 1997 at Montana Studio in Richmond, Avail's fourth album names Lombardy St. and Scuffle Town. Pitchfork called it the apotheosis of Avail's sound.
years.xp:
The line-up was Barry, Banks, Gwomper, Erik Larson and Beau Beau on backing vocals. Banks built the intro of Deepwood on a Boss drum machine, writing the lick on bass before moving it to guitar.

Barry told Decibel that hardcore kids, leftist political fans and pop-punk crowds all started turning up at the same Avail shows. Pitchfork's Zach Baron gave it 7.7. In May 2019 Decibel inducted it into its Hall of Fame as a melodic hardcore classic.

years.src: Wikipedia: One Wrench · Discogs · edtrask.com · Razorcake #14
years.h: One Wrench: Avail's first Fat album, with Ed Trask on drums
years.p: Recorded in March 2000 at Montana Studio in Richmond with Mark Miley, with Richmond muralist [[Ed Trask|0cf5525b-a45c-4e1d-b269-d306b793d442]] now on drums. The Pittsburgh Post-Gazette called Avail undersung working-class heroes.
years.xp: Avail's Fat run began with the 100 Times EP in 1999. Trask, a 1992 VCU painting graduate, kept painting illegal murals on tour and became one of Richmond's best-known muralists. Erik Larson, Avail's drummer since Satiate, went on to Alabama Thunderpussy.

q: I have no idea what Beau does but he does everything
years.h: Beau Beau Butler: no instrument, all the injuries
years.p: Avail's cheerleader, a friend of Tim Barry's since kindergarten, played nothing and did everything: shirtless, often missing a tooth, stage-diving and working the pit. He has broken bones and chipped teeth doing it.
years.xp:
Barry told Decibel that Beau started out sitting beside the drum riser and simply began stage diving; nobody gave him the job. Barry calls him critic, fifth songwriter and crowd motivator. He is credited as Cheerleader on Satiate as early as 1991.

Asked by Punknews, Avail said Barry and Beau had been hurt in the crowd and on stage more times than they could count: cuts, broken bones, chipped teeth, stitches.

years.src: Wikipedia: Front Porch Stories · Fat Wreck Chords · Riot Fest
years.h: Front Porch Stories: Avail's last album so far
years.p: Recorded in June 2002 at Sound of Music in Richmond with producer Bryan Paulson and released on Fat. It carried the motto Ride fast, live slow, which Tim Barry still uses.
years.xp: Fat's bio from this period says Avail spent about a third of each year jammed in a van. Around the same time Simple Song, from 4am Friday, turned up on the Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 4 soundtrack.

eras.title: Food Not Bombs, freight trains and a quiet exit
eras.text: Avail was a working band giving its hometown money away, while Tim Barry rode freight trains and started singing alone with an acoustic guitar. Jade Tree reissued the Lookout! albums in 2006, no new album came, and in 2007 the band simply stopped.

years.h: Avail gives every Richmond show's take to Food Not Bombs
years.p: Tim Barry told Razorcake that Avail donated all the proceeds from its Richmond shows to the local Food Not Bombs chapter, which he had seen founded a decade earlier.
years.xp: In the same interview Barry described riding freight out of Richmond's ACCA yard, a habit learned from a friend he called Ronny Richmond. He called it voluntary homelessness, and said it fed his songs.

years.h: Tim Barry starts playing solo folk sets
years.p: Tim Barry began performing acoustic folk on his own in 2004, which led to Rivanna Junction on Chunksaah in 2006 and a solo catalog that outlasted Avail's first run.

q: I wasn't having any fun. There was too much tension in the van.
years.h: Avail stops playing, with tension in the van and $250 each
years.p: Avail played its last shows in 2007 without announcing a breakup. Tim Barry later told Vice the fun was gone and the van was tense; the last tour paid each member $250 for ten days.
years.xp:
Everyone was working several jobs. A New York fan named Pete, who had seen every Avail show in the city since ABC No Rio, told Barry he could tell something was wrong at the final Knitting Factory show.

Barry told RVA Magazine in 2019 there were not many layers to it: playing just was not as fun as it once was. During the break Banks and others played in Freeman.

eras.title: Back at The National
eras.text: Twelve years after its last show, Avail sold out The National in Richmond in seconds and kept going: a second night, a Decibel Hall of Fame nod, Hot Water Music dates and a Satiate reissue.

years.h: Beau Beau Butler announces a run for mayor of Richmond
years.p: Avail's hype man told Vice he would run for mayor in 2016, promising $2 highballs, a ban on Crocs and flip-flops, and a website shaming bad tippers.

years.h: Avail announces one reunion show, then adds a second
years.p: Tim Barry agreed after listening to Over the James with his daughters around its 20th anniversary. The July 19 date at The National sold out in about ten seconds; a July 20 show followed.
years.xp:
Barry told Beau Butler he would play if all he had to do was write the setlist and sing. Butler passed it on to the others. Iron Reagan quietly lent the band practice space, and Barry showed up to the first practice without warming up.

Tickets for the second night were sold in person at the venue, and Barry drove past with his daughters to see the line. They sold out within hours.

years.h: Avail's reunion at The National opens with South Bound 95
years.p: Tim Barry, Joe Banks, Gwomper, Erik Larson and Beau Beau Butler played their first show in 12 years. Beau brought foam fingers, Super Soakers and a novelty cowboy hat.
years.xp: Stereogum's Tom Breihan reported a crowd mostly in its forties and fifties and a band playing with full intensity. A few songs in, Barry told the room it felt good.

years.h: Satiate gets a 30th anniversary reissue and Hot Water Music dates
years.p: Avail reissued its debut itself, the first Satiate vinyl in about 15 years, and played Carrboro, Atlanta and St. Petersburg with [[Hot Water Music|c83907ee-8b5a-4547-8f68-96572243ea7f]].
